articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion
articles.title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion
articles.text:
Anthropic intends to push ahead with its IPO despite shakier markets and the broader pullback from AI investing.

The Claude-maker said in an updated IPO filing on Tuesday that it would be offering a total of 825 million Class A shares at an estimated price range of $70 to $78 per share. The sale is expected to raise anywhere from $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion.

The company could end up being worth a hefty $1.404 trillion if its shares list at the top of the price range, on a fully diluted basis. That would represent a significant jump up from the $965 billion valuation Anthropic reached in a May fundraise, but it’s still lower than the $2 trillion the company was reportedly targeting a couple months ago.

Separately, Anthropic said it had struck a deal to privately sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC. Google and Nvidia are investing $10 billion apiece.

All up, Anthropic estimates net proceeds to reach somewhere between $84.6 billion and $93.7 billion (the latter if the IPO underwriters exercise their option to buy additional shares).

Underwriters, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, will have the option to buy up to 123.75 million more shares from Anthropic at the IPO price.

As a public benefit corporation, the founders hold a Class F share with 50.1% of the voting power. The Long-Term Benefit Trust will also elect a board majority, so Class A buyers will have limited influence.

Anthropic intends to start trading on the Nasdaq close to November 19, per reporting from CNBC, under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The company expects up to 20% of the offering to be allocated to retail investors.

Anthropic also gave out a few new details in the updated filing. The company said its run-rate revenue reached $81 billion by the end of October, about $10 billion more than at the end of September.

Also, the filing now lists how many shares the company’s co-founders expect to sell in the IPO: CEO Dario Amodei, president and chairperson Daniela Amodei, chief compute officer Tom Brown, Anthropic Institute head Jack Clark, chief science officer Jared Kaplan, chief architect Sam McCandlish, and interpretability research lead Christopher Olah are all selling nearly 3.4 million shares each. At the $74 midpoint of the IPO price range, that would land them about $250 million each.

The updated filing also has a small but important change that hints at the company’s stance toward the Trump administration: The company at many points uses “super intelligence” and “SI” interchangeably with “artificial intelligence” and “AI,” citing Trump’s executive order from September that directed government departments and agencies to use that new terminology to refer to AI.

The company’s third-quarter revenue came in at $17 billion, and nine-month revenue was $33.2 billion. The company reported a nine-month net loss of $104 billion, with compute and infrastructure commitments hitting $900.9 billion. It has nearly $132 billion in cash and short-term investments.

OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after it raised $11 billion, nearly half the $20 billion it had first tried to raise.

Note: This story has been updated with additional details and color from the updated IPO filing.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Carbon is now available

Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model.

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.Two weeks ago, we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program. Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price

1
as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search.

Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysisAcross legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model.

In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding.

Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI designCarbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding.

Frontier cybersecurity capabilitiesGemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches.Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice.In Project Fortify, Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem.Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit. By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes.As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies.

Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoningGemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs.Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work:Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal. Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. The result indicates Carbon’s potential to unlock scalable formal verification, long considered a gold-standard approach to building secure software.Enzyme assay development: Provided with only lab notebooks and raw data, Carbon went beyond standard analysis to surface hard-to-interpret data anomalies, which it used to diagnose subtle wet lab experimental artifacts such as incomplete automated mixing in deep wells, leading to substantially improved reproducibility. Moreover Carbon improved methods to deconvolute chromatography peaks and caught trace sample carryover in research instruments, significantly accelerating the development of new assays and tightening the feedback loop between computation and the bench.Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. For example, across 7 low-homolog protein families from the CASP17 blind test set, Carbon increased the number of homologs retrieved by 40-fold on average, greatly increasing the information available to structure prediction models without need for retraining. While broader benchmarking is still underway, addressing this upstream search bottleneck potentially offers a promising path toward modeling hard-to-characterize regions of the proteome.Four weeks ago, we opened applications to give 10,000 scientists access to Argon in Google Antigravity free of charge for six months to accelerate the pace of their research, and we’ve onboarded thousands of scientists already. Today, we’re expanding access to Carbon for current and future participants, and going forward, the program will continue providing access to our latest frontier models as they become available. Applications remain open and onboarding continues on a weekly rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.

Progress in model safety and securityWith each new model release, we continue to strengthen our safety and security mitigations, agentic misuse prevention, model alignment, and harm reduction proportionately with model capability.Because Gemini 4 Carbon introduces stronger cyber capabilities we build on Argon’s strong safety and security stack to fortify robustness to misuse and prompt injection.Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks: We’ve strengthened our misuse safeguards to help ensure stronger defensive reasoning does not translate into offensive risk. In simulated cyberattack testing environments seeded with ExploitBench and CyScenarioBench, Carbon blocked 99% of attack trajectories from our adaptive red-teaming agent that can iteratively revisit its attack plans after each block. The Carbon safeguards lowered the per-attempt breach rate to just 0.8% (down from 3.1% on Argon). Our safeguards also lowered the automated cyberattack query success rate to 2.17% in Gray Swan’s testing, compared to 9.86% on Argon. And external testing by Trajectory Labs found zero new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests.Promoting safe and aligned model interactions: When we announced Carbon, we showed significant improvements in alignment as measured by our monitor flag rates across the model’s lifecycle, as well as reductions in data fabrication. New results show that on our 375-task agentic honesty benchmark, it passed 92% of tasks (compared to 70% for Argon) — declining to fill in missing experimental data 98% of the time and flagging methodological flaws 68% of the time.

Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: Two weeks ago, we shared that Carbon achieved a 0% prompt injection attack success rate on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark — marking the first time that milestone has been reached. At the same time, we know that prompt injection robustness remains an area for continued improvement. Our advanced automated red teaming continues to push the limits here and has shown that models could be further improved against sophisticated attacks in some distributions. It provides the data for us to continuously advance our models’ security to the next frontier.For more details, read the full Gemini 4 Carbon Safety and Security report.

articles.sourceTitle: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
articles.title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
articles.text:
I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it.
I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers.
Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame.
In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications.
By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop.

Four ways AI makes codebases fragile
Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase.
1. AI writes shallow tests
One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric.
2. AI writes overly complex ccode
AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand.
3. Reliance on AI decreases human understanding
And that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures.
4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar
AI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code.
Four signs that you have a fragile codebase
If you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase.
1. AI generated codebases have more incidents
When you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers.
2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebases
Not only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve.
3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to users
When humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing.
4. AI results in a poor user experience
And that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification.
Products made for humans require a human touch
The fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI.

articles.sourceTitle: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
articles.title: thisisme6598/gemini_files: Documentation of Gemini File Leaking Behavior · GitHub
articles.text:
Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
Clarification (Nov 10, 2026): Scope & Account Applicability.
This documentation and technical reproduction apply strictly to Consumer Google Accounts (personal @gmail.com accounts) governed by the standard Gemini Apps Privacy Notice, Gemini Apps Activity, and Google Help Answer 16836988. Google Workspace commercial accounts (Business, Enterprise, and Education) operate under separate Cloud Data Processing Addenda (DPA) that contractually exclude human review and external generative training by default.
In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers".
Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost, Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."
Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic.

When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups.
Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic, running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios:

Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query.

Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight").

Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures.

Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context.

If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline--you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again.

Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings.

Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better.

Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about).

If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above.

To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history.
I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number"]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers.
Final Comments and Caveats
Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data, including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject).
Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.
